Read and prepare a species detection matrix

Source: R/read_matrix.R
read_matrix.Rd

Read and prepare a species detection matrix

Usage

read_matrix(
  data,
  timestep = 1,
  time_range = NULL,
  baseline = NULL,
  baseline_min_species = NULL
)

Arguments

data

A CSV file path or a numeric or logical detection matrix. In a CSV, the first column contains species names and remaining column names contain starting years. In a matrix, species names must be row names and starting years must be column names; do not include a species column inside the matrix. Detection values must be 0/1 or, for a logical matrix, FALSE/TRUE. Missing values are not allowed.

timestep

Positive output interval width, in years. Defaults to 1.

time_range

Optional numeric vector of length two giving inclusive limits on output interval labels.

baseline

Optional starting interval label within the selected range.

baseline_min_species

Optional positive integer. Select the first interval in the selected range with at least this many detected species.

Value

A numeric 0/1 matrix with species row names and time column names. A preparation attribute records the input type, input interval width, output interval width, retained labels, baseline selection and coverage. Coverage endpoints use an exclusive upper bound. The returned matrix has class modgee_matrix; printing shows only matrix entries and row/column names. Preparation metadata remain accessible through attr(M, "preparation"). Existing informational messages are retained.

Details

At least two time columns are required. Column names must represent finite positive integers (zero, negative and fractional years are rejected). Integer-valued numeric forms such as 2000.0 are accepted. The names represent the starting years of consecutive, equally spaced observation intervals. The input interval width is inferred from the spacing between column names. Missing observation intervals must not be omitted from the input. Equally spaced labels are interpreted as consecutive intervals, not isolated years.

The output width must be an integer multiple of the input width. An invalid width error reports both the supplied timestep and input width. Input intervals must fit within calendar-aligned output intervals without crossing their boundaries. Output labels follow floor(time / timestep) * timestep. For input labels 1900, 1910, 1920, use timestep = 10 to retain the original interval width. Such data cannot be split into annual records.

Processing proceeds in this order: aggregate intervals, apply time_range, then select the baseline. Aggregation records whether a species was detected at least once within each output interval. The upper bound of time_range refers to an interval label, not its ending year. If the requested range extends beyond the available output labels but overlaps them, the overlap is retained with an informational message reporting the retained label range before baseline selection. A range with no overlapping labels is an error.

Invalid time labels are reported with their original names and positions. Duplicate years are compared numerically, so 1900 and 1900.0 are duplicates. Time-column positions exclude the species-name column in a CSV.

baseline and baseline_min_species are mutually exclusive. If neither is supplied, the first selected interval is used. All-zero species rows and the original species order are retained. Incomplete boundary intervals are retained with an informational message. For annual input ending in 2026 and timestep = 10, the column labelled 2020 summarizes only 2020–2026. Unobserved years are not added.

Existing custom attributes on matrix input are not carried forward. Preparation information is recalculated from the supplied time columns. For already aggregated data, the original coverage of a partial interval cannot be recovered from its starting-year label alone; each input column is interpreted as covering one full inferred input interval.

Usage Examples


# Read annual records from the installed CSV.
M_annual <- read_matrix(data = example_file)

# Aggregate into ten-year intervals and select the baseline.
M <- read_matrix(
  data = example_file,
  timestep = 10,
  baseline_min_species = 10
)
dim(M)
attr(M, "preparation")

# Prepare an existing matrix instead of a CSV file.
M_decadal <- read_matrix(data = M_annual, timestep = 10)

# Keep a specified range of interval labels.
M_range <- read_matrix(
  data = example_file, timestep = 10,
  time_range = c(1900, 2000)
)

# Specify the baseline directly.
M_baseline <- read_matrix(
  data = example_file, timestep = 10,
  baseline = 1900
)

# Apply a detection threshold within a selected time range.
M_selected <- read_matrix(
  data = example_file, timestep = 10,
  time_range = c(1900, 2020),
  baseline_min_species = 10
)

See also

Functions: fit_modgee, plot_modgee, save_result

Examples: example_file, example_M, example_groups, example_result, example_grouped_result, example_bootstrap_result

Console display

Every successful call prints the prepared matrix, including calls assigned to a variable. The complete matrix is returned invisibly to avoid duplicate automatic printing; preparation metadata are retained but not displayed.
